utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now, finally we can start with a joint Status Conference, and the first point has to be, of course, as there is admittedly some undue delay, the question of the situation of the three accused in the detention unit. Do you want to address some issues as regards to this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the accused Obrenovic has nothing to say on this point at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleagues from the Prosecution, at this point in time, we have no comments to make until we have received the amended indictment, but I would just like to say that I have prepared a brief on behalf of the accused Jokic seeking his provisional release because he surrendered himself to the Tribunal voluntarily on the 15th of August. It has been six months since his initial detention, but this will be something that we will discuss separately with the Prosecution on another occasion. I just wanted to announce that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The accused in person, do they want to add something specifically on their health condition, on their situation in the detention unit? Are there any problems you face and want to express in person? No reaction. I thank you. Now, it's, of course, a little bit difficult to go on with the proceedings, but I'm quite sure that we will be faced in time with a joint indictment. And I'm hesitant, if this is the time now to discuss possible issues of this amended indictment to avoid the exchange of other briefs in preparation or in response to the amended indictment. We all have the draft, and I wonder if it wouldn't be the case just if the word draft would be redacted from this document. From the side of the Defence counsels, are there any objections or arguments with regard to this draft?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the accused Obrenovic, we are not prepared to address that today. We have been waiting to see what the final indictment looks like. It has -- the proposed indictment has been amended several times, and Mr. McCloskey has indicated that there may be possibly some other indictments, so we would prefer to wait until we have the final document and proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comments. We support fully the stand taken by my colleague, Mr. Wilson. Once we have received the indictment, we will decide on any possible motions or objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nothing to add, Your Honour. I do agree with counsel for Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. From my point of view, I would indeed appreciate if this draft could be amended in the light of the Kupreskic decision, and I would prefer if we could have some more details, some more precise details what is really the -- the factual basis we are working with. For example, in paragraph 15, in the end, a lot has been said on what happened in July 1995 in general, and then reference is made only to acts of the accused. I would appreciate that we have more clear indication what the Office of the Prosecutor regards as "acts" for which the accused are indubitably criminally responsible. I enjoyed this morning to learn a lot about the different approach the Office of the Prosecutor has, for example, with regard to Mr. Jokic and the two other accused. But we have to know what is the real basis, and we have to know this in order to describe very precisely what is the issue of this case, and thereby giving the Defence the opportunity really to protect their interests when -- and they can do this only when they know what is the real factual basis. Another point, it goes to preciseness, we can find in the amendment -- for example, in point 26.7, there the persons killed are named. This is not the case in the framework of 26.2(A), (B), (C), (D). For clarification, from my point of view, it would indeed be better, if not necessary, that also here we have the names of persons been killed on these accusations. And this is true for the entire draft. Of course, I'm aware that some points can be left open until we have the Pre-Trial Brief, but whatever can be done now already in the indictment should be done in order to have the appropriate reactions of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Defence counsels and of the accused, of course. As regards the time schedule to be expected now, we should be aware that we have a lot of courtroom space available as from March. I'm quite sure it will not be possible to have this case ripe for starting in March, but we all should try to envisage a start of this trial possibly in April already. There would be a possibility, and with respect to the situations of the accused in detention pending trial, we should do whatever we can to have this case started as soon as possible. The arrangements, of course, should be left, and have to be left, until we have the new joint indictment, and we get the first reactions from your side. Then in a 65 ter meeting in mid-February, we should try to find a time schedule aiming at the start of this case in mid-April 2002. Any comments from the parties? Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing, Mr. President. The Prosecution is ready to proceed in mid-April. We have a large volume of material that we continue to give to the Defence, so much so that they, I think, are working hard to read it all. But that's the only problem I see. And if -- we will get that material -- continue to get that material to them as quick as we can, but the Prosecution is ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the side of the Defence counsels?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Speaking for Mr. Obrenovic, Your Honour, the Defence, as per Mr. Obrenovic, would have difficulty beginning as early as April. We are still receiving discovery materials from the Prosecution, and I am told by them - we have another meeting this afternoon - that there remains a considerably large amount of materials for us to receive and have an opportunity to review, discuss with the client, and prepare for the case. I can understand that the Prosecution is ready to go to trial. They've had something like a four- or five-year head start. They have also tried this case, essentially, with the Krstic case. We have not had those advantages. And I am very sensitive to the fact that my client is detained, and we certainly have no intention to have him in a pre-trial detention status any longer than necessary, but I'm very concerned that a starting date of April or mid-April would be extremely difficult for us to prepare for, given the amount of materials provided to us. The Krstic case, for instance, Your Honour, has a transcript of some 12.000 pages. I have been reading that religiously. That is only part of the materials. As I'm sure the Prosecution would agree, there are thousands of pages of documents that go with that. There is a limited amount that any attorney can absorb of such volumes of material. We're doing our very best to do that. I'm working on essentially nothing but Mr. Obrenovic's case at this time. But speaking for him, I believe that I would have great difficulty being ready to go to trial in April and to represent him as he deserves to be represented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these clear words. The other Defence counsels, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly, Your Honour, I did not expect that we would be discussing April, the date of April now, especially in light of the fact that we still do not have the amended indictment. I don't think that there will be any substantial amendments as to the factual description and the legal qualification of the acts my client is charged with, but the only problem that I foresee would be if we were to receive a great volume of documents or witness statements in the forthcoming months, statements of witnesses that the Prosecution interviewed in the past two months, if I'm not mistaken. In preparing for the Defence of Dragan Jokic, we estimate that the statements of these witnesses are very important, and it seems to us that it would be quite difficult to give an estimate as to the beginning of the trial without having seen these statements first. Secondly, we think that the Butler report - and as far as we know, he's still making some more specific clarifications that pertain to this particular case - without that, it would be very hard to give you an answer, but as regards the defence of my client, we feel that the Butler report should also contain information about the responsibilities and duties of the duty officer in the brigade, according to the regulations valid in the VRS in 1995, because these are directly related to five counts of the existing indictment, that is, the indictment that was valid to this date against my client. I also support what my colleague Mr. Wilson has said. I couldn't give you an answer as to the trial date in mid-April, year 2002, but of course, after we have received the amended indictment, we will be able to give you a more specific answer on the date that you proposed, that is, mid-February. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't want to repeat what my colleagues have said, but the problem that we have at this moment Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is that there's a great deal of discovery that has yet to be brought to us, and it would be very difficult to gauge what will be needed, specifically because we need to do investigation, and one cannot do a proper investigation until they know what they're investigating, because I believe, in representing Mr. Blagojevic, that we need to look into everything, all the details, and take a very serious look at every allegation that is being presented by the Prosecutor's office. It's my understanding that Mr. Butler is preparing a more specific report regarding the Srebrenica incident. The first report -- actually, he prepared two reports, one in general, one more specific, but the specific report with respect to Srebrenica dealt with the corps command and not the brigade command, and though it may not be that much work, I don't know at what time we're going to get it, and of course we will need to have it examined by our own experts. So it would be very difficult to say, but I can, I guess with some degree of confidence, inform the Court that it would be virtually impossible to go ahead in mid-April and afford Mr. Blagojevic effective assistance of counsel given the amount of material that we are receiving and we are still receiving. Additionally, I should point out that there are a large number of intercepts that have not been translated. I know some may be in a process of being translated. Some, there may be no intention of having them translated, but nonetheless, they have been provided to us, and we are looking into those intercepts. Additionally, we have made repeated, and I underscore the word "repeated," efforts with the Registrar's Office to supply computer access to Mr. Blagojevic so he can review and look at these intercepts. It's my understanding that Mr. Obrenovic has access to a computer and has been assisting his Defence counsel, as he should, and we believe that in all due fairness, Mr. Blagojevic should also have equal opportunity. Moreover, the Krstic trial has not been translated into the B/C/S. Mr. Blagojevic does not read English. We have received all the tapes from the trial, and of course it behooves Mr. Blagojevic to listen to at least selective portions of that trial. Again, we are of the opinion, particularly since Mr. Blagojevic is in custody, that we go to trial as expeditiously as possible, and in order to do so, Mr. Blagojevic is prepared and has been assisting us on a full-time basis. In other words, he is part of the Defence team, fully engaged in reading all of the material and coming up to speed with all the of the facts in this case. And so given the amount of material, given the fact that we don't have a computer yet available for him to participate in looking over these intercepts -- and again, I might add that we're talking about military operations, and someone who was from the inside obviously can shed a lot more light than someone just reading it from the outside. We will continue to press the Registrar's office. They are unwilling to provide equipment to listen to the tapes. We will do that. But we have been given assurances that they will provide us with a computer. They have yet to do so. To the extent that this Court could assist, we would welcome any assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this very important contribution. Question to the Office of the Prosecutor: Are there any obstacles from their point of view in order to facilitate proceedings? Of course, all the three accused should have access to a computer, and they should have the possibility, in order to avoid unnecessary translations, access to the tapes of the Krstic trial in B/C/S. What's your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Wilson and I anticipated this problem as early as August, and we put in a joint request for the Registry to have a computer set up for Mr. Obrenovic, who I think was the only accused at the time. And then with the other accused, the Prosecution has spoken to the Registry several times trying to also get this set up for the other accused, because the information that we are providing to the Defence is sensitive Prosecution information files. And we, in speaking with the head of the detention unit, he was prepared to provide -- or if he is provided a computer, set up a situation where accused could in privacy review this material and not download it or copy it or anything like that, but review it. But that they needed an order from the Registry. So we made this request. We got a response back from the Registry saying that, "Well, we hear that Mr. Obrenovic has his own, so that solves the issue." Of course, it doesn't solve the issue. Mr. Karnavas is absolutely right. So any help we can all get to solve this problem, I think, would be appreciated on all sides because each counsel has invoked reciprocal discovery. And the Prosecutor's office did search both the Bratunac Brigade and the Zvornik Brigade, and the volumes of material that the defendants would naturally want to have access to is being provided to them. But it would help to get this going if they had computers. And it would also assist the Prosecution in the security of this material and that it remain private, that it be something that would be administered by the Detention Centre and not just left up to individual laptops, which is the way it is now, which we're satisfied with for the time being but we're hoping that the Detention Centre and the Registry would solve this problem. Regarding Mr. Butler's report, Mr. Butler is working on that report. And hopefully, that report will be done in due course. Perhaps the statements today will help him be inspired to get it done as early as possible, although he is working on several cases. But we will try to get that out as soon as possible. And we will meet with Defence counsel today to continue to get the material to them. It's not a question of them not receiving the material. I'm sure they would all agree that they have more material than they can possibly even digest right now. We have provided them with CDs of the complete Krstic transcript. We are in the process of providing some of the some 1.000 exhibits from Krstic. And since it's not in B/C/S, we have provided the - I don't know - many, many audiotapes for the clients to review in B/C/S. And with that in mind, it is a process that I know everyone is fully engaged in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these comments. I can see that there is a joint motion of the Office of the Prosecutor and of the Defence counsels for having computer equipment and audiotape players. For me, it seems self-evident, but I am really grateful for your contribution. I will do what I can to grant access to these computers and tape players immediately. It's quite clear what you said. Of course, you have to know what it's all about. And of course, then you can start with your Defence. And we are all committed to the principle of a fair trial, and we can't start earlier. But part of this principle of fair trial is, of course, to have expeditious proceedings, especially when we have three persons in detention pending trial. And therefore, I would all of you invite, indeed, to contribute to an envisaged time schedule which should be discussed at a 65 ter meeting mid-February, to come as soon as possible to the trial stage in this case. Are there any other contributions for the Status Conference right now? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you all for this work and spirit of cooperation this morning, and I hope we can continue in this spirit in future. And the conference is now adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
